name: Battle of Pydna
info: Roman legions under the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus defeated King Perseus of Macedon and his phalanx near Pydna in 168 BCE, in the Third Macedonian War, ending the Antigonid line of kings and Macedonian independence.

facts.date: 22 June 168 BCE; the fighting began in the afternoon
facts.place: A fairly level plain near Katerini, a village south of Pydna, below the foothills of Mount Olocrus in Macedonia, northern Greece
facts.sides: Rome and its allies under the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus, at least 28,600 men and up to 37,000; Macedon under King Perseus, 43,000 soldiers at the start of the war and closer to 30,000 by the time of the battle
facts.outcome: The Roman legions broke the Macedonian phalanx; Perseus fled, nearly 11,000 Macedonians were captured, and Livy reported that his sources claimed up to 20,000 Macedonian dead.

t: The Romans fought with two legions in the centre and allied infantry on the flanks, and the Macedonians with a pike phalanx and an elite guard of 3,000.
The phalanx lost its cohesion as it advanced over rough ground in the foothills, and Paullus ordered the legions into the gaps to attack the phalangites on their exposed flanks.
Perseus was later paraded in triumph in Rome in chains, the Macedonian kingdom was dissolved into four republics, and Macedonia in time became a Roman province.
dyk: The night before the battle there was a lunar eclipse, which the Macedonians perceived as an ill omen; according to Plutarch, they took it as a sign of their king's demise.
ev: The Third Macedonian War starts after acts by King Perseus of Macedon lead Rome to declare war
Perseus wins the Battle of Callinicus and regains most of his losses, including the city of Dion
Lucius Aemilius Paullus takes command of the Roman force and sends Scipio Nasica on a march round the Macedonian position
Perseus withdraws north to a plain near Katerini, south of Pydna, suited to the phalanx
The Roman legions break the Macedonian phalanx at Pydna and the pursuit lasts until nightfall
Perseus later surrenders to Paullus and is taken to Rome and paraded in triumph in chains
Paullus attacks Epirus, enslaving 150,000 Epirotes and sacking 70 cities

sections.background:
The Third Macedonian War started in 171 BCE, after a number of acts on the part of King Perseus of Macedon incited Rome to declare war. At first the Romans won a number of small victories, largely because Perseus refused to consolidate his armies. By the end of the year the tide had changed: Perseus had won the Battle of Callinicus and regained most of his losses, including the important religious city of Dion. He then established himself in an unassailable position on the river Elpeus, in north-eastern Greece.

The next year command of the Roman expeditionary force passed to Lucius Aemilius Paullus, an experienced soldier and one of the consuls for the year. To force Perseus from his position, Paullus sent a small force of 8,200 foot and 120 horse under Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum to the coast, as a feint to convince Perseus that he was attempting a flanking manoeuvre by river. Instead, that night Scipio took his force south and over the mountains to the west of both armies, as far as Pythion, and then swung north-east to attack the Macedonians from the rear.

A Roman deserter reached the Macedonian camp, and Perseus sent a force of 12,000 under Milo to block the approach road. The encounter that followed sent Milo and his men back in disarray towards the main Macedonian army. Perseus then moved north and took up a position near Katerini, a village south of Pydna, on a fairly level plain that suited the phalanx.
sections.forces:
The Romans had at least 28,600 men and up to 37,000, of whom 22,000 to 34,000 were infantry: Romans, Italians, and allies from Greece, Numidia and Liguria, and possibly Hispania. The Macedonians had 43,000 soldiers at the start of the war, of whom more than 20,000 were phalangites. By the time of the battle the Macedonian army numbered closer to 30,000. Before the battle Perseus had dispatched 8,000 Macedonians (2,000 peltasts, 5,000 phalangites and 1,000 cavalry) to guard against the Roman fleet threatening his rear.

The cavalry forces were roughly equal: up to 4,000 Macedonians and Thracians against some 3,400 Romans and allies. The two armies were drawn up in their usual fashion. The Romans placed their two legions in the middle, with the allied Latin, Italian and Greek infantry on their flanks and the cavalry on the wings. The Roman right was supplemented by 22 war elephants.

The phalanx took up the centre of the Macedonian line, with the elite Guard, 3,000 strong, formed to its left. Lighter peltasts, mercenaries and Thracian infantry guarded the two flanks of the phalanx, and the Macedonian cavalry was most probably arrayed on both flanks. The stronger contingent was on the Macedonian right, where Perseus commanded the heavy cavalry, including his elite Sacred Squadron, and the Thracian Odrysian cavalry were deployed.
sections.course:
Paullus had brought Scipio back to the main force, while Perseus deployed for what appeared to be an attack from the south by Scipio. The Roman armies were in fact to the west, and when they advanced they found Perseus fully deployed. Instead of joining battle with troops tired from the march, the Romans encamped to the west, in the foothills of Mount Olocrus. The night before the battle there was a lunar eclipse. Paullus is said to have understood that eclipses occurred at regular intervals but still thought it necessary to perform sacrifices and wait for favourable omens.

The fighting began on the afternoon of 22 June. One story is that Paullus waited until late enough in the day for the sun not to be in his troops' eyes and then sent an unbridled horse forward to cause alarm; more likely it began when some Roman foragers came too close and were attacked by Thracians in Perseus' army. The two centres engaged at about 3 pm, a short distance from the Roman camp. The Roman allies tried to beat down the enemy pikes or hack off their points, with little success, and the Romans used a planned retreat over the rough ground.

As the phalanx pushed forward into the foothills the ground grew more uneven and the line lost its cohesion. Paullus ordered the legions into the gaps, attacking the phalangites on their exposed flanks, where the longer Roman sword and heavier shield prevailed at close quarters. They were soon joined by the Roman right, which had routed the Macedonian left. Perseus fled with the cavalry on the Macedonian right. The 3,000-strong Guard fought to the death. The battle lasted about an hour, and the pursuit lasted until nightfall.
sections.aftermath:
Nearly 11,000 Macedonians were captured, and Livy reported that his various sources claimed up to 20,000 Macedonian dead. Among the Romans, Paullus' son Scipio Aemilianus was thought lost for a while but had been pursuing the retreating Macedonians with some friends, and Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus, the son of Cato the Elder, distinguished himself in a combat in which he first lost and finally recovered his sword.

The political consequences were severe. Perseus later surrendered to Paullus, was paraded in triumph in Rome in chains and was then imprisoned. The Senate's settlement included the deportation to Italy of many of the king's friends and the imprisonment, later house arrest, of Perseus at Alba Fucens. The Macedonian kingdom was dissolved and its government replaced with four republics, which were heavily restricted from intercourse or trade with one another. In time these were also dissolved and Macedonia became a Roman province.

In 167 BCE Paullus received orders to attack Epirus, which resulted in the enslavement of 150,000 Epirotes and the sacking of 70 cities. This happened because the Molossians, one tribe of the Epirote League, had sent aid to Perseus, but all the Epirotes suffered alike in the Roman attack. The victory was celebrated in Athens, where an inscribed decree of the Council and People in 168 BCE honours Calliphanes, an Athenian citizen who had been present with the Roman and Attalid armies at Pydna, for bringing news of the victory to Athens.
sections.sources:
Several named writers report parts of the battle. Plutarch tells how the Macedonians read the eclipse and that the surviving infantry accused the king and his cavalry of cowardice, having seen the cavalry take no part. Poseidonius claimed that Perseus was injured by missiles and brought to the city of Pydna at the start of the battle. Livy gave the Macedonian dead as up to 20,000 according to his various sources, and Paullus himself later claimed that the sight of the phalanx filled him with alarm and amazement.

The accounts disagree on several points. The exact cause of the start of the fighting is disputed. Other sources state that the cavalry did not take part, because of a strike against Perseus by the nobles, and others that a corps of 10,000 Macedonians was cut off through confusion or a tactical error by the king and did not take part in the engagement. Estimates of both armies' strengths are ranges, and the Macedonian figure fell during the war.
sections.legacy:
The battle saw the further ascendancy of Rome in the Hellenistic world and the end of the Antigonid line of kings, whose power traced back to Antigonus Monophthalmus, one of Alexander the Great's Diadochi. It was not the final conflict between the two rivals, but it broke the back of Macedonian power. The battle and its political aftermath mark the effective end of Macedonian independence, although formal annexation was still some years away.

The battle is often considered a victory of the flexibility of the Roman legion's manipular system over the rigidity of the Macedonian phalanx. The case of the 3,000 Agema peltasts, who kept their cohesion far longer than the regular phalanx, has been taken to show that the training of the troops played an important part in determining both the frontal strength of the pike phalanx and the success of infantry trying to break through the pike wall.

summary: At Pydna on 22 June 168 BCE the legions of the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus broke the Macedonian phalanx of King Perseus, who fled. The kingdom was dissolved, Perseus was paraded in Rome in chains, and the Antigonid line of kings ended.
notes: The article's date is written 'June 22' in the text and '168 BC' in the lead; I gave 22 June 168 BCE. The article names no consul year for Paullus; 'the next year' follows 171 BCE only loosely, so the background says 'the next year' as the article does.
The article says Perseus 'later surrendered to Paullus' without a date; the ev entry is dated 168 BCE as an approximation of 'later' and could be changed to 'after 168 BCE'.

Self-contradictory: the article has Perseus' cavalry on the Macedonian right under his command, and then says other sources state the cavalry did not fight because of a strike by the nobles; Plutarch has Perseus' cavalry yet to engage. I kept both versions in the sources section.

The article says the Romans' 8,200 foot and 120 horse went 'to the coast' as a feint; Scipio's march ends 'to attack from the rear' but the article never says it arrived or what it did. I left that out of the course.

The article gives the Macedonian figure of 8,000 detached against the Roman fleet as a separate example, and 30,000 by the time of the battle; whether the 30,000 is before or after the detachment is not stated.

'Roman allies' officers' anecdote (garments rent, standard thrown among the enemy) left out for length. The article's Roman total of 'at least 28,600, up to 37,000' with infantry of 22,000 to 34,000 is as given.
The legacy section is short because the article says little of memory or monuments beyond the Athenian decree (placed in the aftermath) and the manipular-versus-phalanx view.
The 'forces' section's position of the Roman 'allied Latin, Italian, and Greek infantry' on the flanks is as written in the article.
